issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette: At eighty, Hina’s garage smelled of flux and cut aluminum, a scent that usually grounded her but now only sharpened her nerves. She still kept her welding torch on the bench, though she rarely struck an arc anymore. Instead, her afternoons were spent watching the driveway, her eyes tracking every car that slowed too long near her property line. Her nights were no better. She fought sleep until her muscles ached, and when she finally drifted off, a sudden draft or settling house would snap her awake. She would rise without turning on the lights, press her palm against the front door to feel the vibration of the deadbolt, and verify the stove was cold. It was a routine she had built over decades, a quiet architecture of control in a home where she never truly felt safe. She had learned the need for that architecture during her thirties, when her marriage curdled into sustained violence. The turning point was a Tuesday evening in the kitchen, when a misplaced invoice sparked a shouting match that ended with her husband throwing her against the cabinets. The impact drove her onto her back, and she lay there listening to his boots pace the linoleum while he swore he would never leave her again. When he finally walked out a year later, the silence did not bring peace. It brought a heavy, inescapable certainty that her body was permanently broken. The scar tissue across her ribs ached before every storm, a constant reminder of shattered cartilage. Worse than the pain was the hollowed-out feeling in her chest; she mourned the loss of her capacity for simple joy, certain she would never feel normal emotions again. She had come to trust her own body less with every passing year, viewing her own nervous system as an unreliable betrayer that could not be counted on to protect her. This conviction in her physical and emotional ruin became the very engine of her hypervigilance. Because she believed her body was fundamentally compromised and untrustworthy, she treated every ordinary sound as a precursor to harm. The groan of her garage door opening, the distant rumble of a truck, the faint tap of a branch against the siding—all of it registered as immediate threat. She stopped inviting her children to the house, telling them she needed quiet, though the truth was she could not bear the risk of an unexpected visitor triggering a panic she knew she would not be able to quiet. She spent her days scanning the perimeter of her garage and home, her shoulders tight, her breath shallow, constantly bracing for a violence she could no longer predict. The exhausting loop only cemented her despair. Lying awake, heart hammering against her damaged ribs, she would spend hours mentally cataloging exits and locks, her nervous system locked in a silent alarm. The chronic sleeplessness drained her affect until the emotional numbness felt absolute. By morning, the relentless alertness convinced her she was truly broken, that her lost capacity for feeling was a permanent sentence rather than a protective freeze. The fear made her body brace, and the bracing made the world feel perpetually dangerous. Now, after thirty years of sleeping with one eye open and moving through her days in a state of quiet dread, Hina sat on her therapist’s couch, her calloused hands twisting in her lap. She had finally made the call because the isolation had become too heavy to carry alone. She told herself she was hoping for a way to finally rest, but what frightened her most was the quiet doubt that some fractures simply never heal.
